Subject: Post-call: streaming & concurrency needs (recap + questions)

Thanks for the call this morning — quick recap from our side and a couple of clarifying questions before we put together an internal pilot plan. High-level PayLance constraints:

- Use case: realtime payment assist and fraud signals in checkout (low-latency streaming responses to user events).
- Target SLO: 95th percentile tail latency <= 250ms for streaming response chunks.
- Expected baseline traffic: 150 req/s steady, with peak bursts to ~700 req/s for short windows (2-5 minutes) during promos.
- Concurrency profile: ~300 concurrent requests at peaks, with many long-running streaming sessions (avg 6-10s). We plan to multiplex multiple short messages per session.
- We prefer HTTP/2 multiplexing over opening many TCP connections; we also need guidance on idle connection limits and client keepalive.

Questions we had:
1) What are Redwood hosted default rate limits / quota primitives for streaming endpoints and how do they behave with HTTP/2 multiplexing?
2) Do you offer dedicated burst capacity or token-bucket increases during events? What’s the lead time?
3) How do connection pool limits map to concurrency tokens — e.g., if a single HTTP/2 connection multiplexes 10 streams, does that count as 10 concurrent requests against quota?

Attaching our short architecture diagram (see doc in follow-up). Happy to run a short pilot if Redwood can provide a scoped quota increase / canary for our integration.

— Evan
Evan Brooks
Head of Platform Engineering, PayLance

Thanks Evan — great to connect. Short answers and proposed next steps below. I’ve also attached our lightweight connpool_playbook.pdf that summarizes how Redwood treats multiplexed streams and quota accounting.

Summary answers:
- Hosted defaults: our public hosted API enforces per-key request-rate and concurrent-stream quotas. Typical default is 120 rps and 60 concurrent streaming sessions per API key for new accounts.
- Multiplexing behavior: Redwood counts active inflight streams as concurrency units. If an HTTP/2 connection carries 10 active streams, that counts as 10 concurrent sessions against the concurrency quota. The per-connection nature (HTTP/2) helps reduce sockets but not concurrency accounting.
- Burst/DED options: we can enable a temporary burst pool for short events (token-bucket style) or move you to a Dedicated reserved capacity pool for predictable peaks. Burst pools can be provisioned within 48–72 business hours for trials; Dedicated requires contract/commit but supports much higher sustained concurrency and guaranteed capacity.
- Idle / keepalive: client keepalive should be <= 60s to avoid idle connection churn; Redwood will close idle streams after 120s by default but that’s configurable for Dedicated customers.

Proposed next steps:
1) We can stand up a 2-week canary with elevated quotas (example proposal attached) scoped to specific API keys and IP ranges.
2) Redwood engineer to run a short load profile (we’ll run the client simulator) to validate 95p <250ms with streaming chunking enabled.
3) If results are good, move to a Dedicated reserved pool or a committed burst arrangement (we’ll provide pricing).

Action items:
- Evan / Priya: confirm target canary dates and any IP ranges.
- We’ll send a quota proposal sheet and a short test plan.

Thanks — looped in Ben on bandwidth/quotas.

— Mina Haddad

Adding some concrete quota options so PayLance can pick a path. Quoting the earlier thread for trace.

Option A — Scoped canary (recommended first step):
- Duration: 14 days
- Elevated limits on specific API keys: 600 rps sustained / 900 rps burst, 400 concurrent streaming sessions, HTTP/2 multiplexing supported.
- Rate limiting: token-bucket with 60s smoothing windows; we’ll enable short burst tokens for 2–5 minute windows.
- Monitoring: we’ll enable per-key latency traces and integrate with your dashboard for the canary.

Option B — Short Dedicated pilot (if you want SLA):
- 1–3 week Dedicated reserved capacity slice: guaranteed 600 rps sustained, 500 concurrent streams, custom idle timeouts.
- Requires order form and standard dedicated onboarding (lead time ~2–3 weeks).

Notes on concurrency accounting: each active stream = 1 concurrency unit. Multiplexing reduces TCP/socket count but does not reduce concurrency accounting unless you implement batching at the application layer so one large request contains multiple logical events. If PayLance can batch smaller events client-side into fewer streaming chunks we can significantly reduce concurrency.

I’ve attached a quick quota-proposal.xlsx with the sample numbers above and an example test ramp. If PayLance confirms the canary window we’ll provision keys and a small playbook for load tests.

Ben Carter
